points: Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a computational method for optimizing a problem.
PSO repeatedly tries to improve a population of candidate solutions according to a measure of quality.
In PSO, each candidate solution is called a particle, and the population is called a swarm.
Basic PSO moves particles through the search space using simple formulas that update their velocities and positions.
A particle's movement is influenced by the best position that particle has found so far.
A particle's movement is also influenced by the best position found so far by any particle in its neighborhood.
The neighborhood can be configured to include the entire swarm.
Updating the best positions as improvements are found is expected to guide the swarm toward good solutions.
PSO is originally attributed to Kennedy and Eberhart.
PSO was originally intended to simulate social behavior.
The original social-behavior model could represent the movement of birds in a flock.
The original social-behavior model could represent the movement of fish in a school.
The original model could also represent changing attitudes in a human population.
Simulating principles of social behavior was found to help solve hard mathematical problems.
Kennedy and Eberhart's book discusses philosophical aspects of PSO and swarm intelligence.
Poli produced an extensive survey of PSO applications.
Bonyadi and Michalewicz published a comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental PSO work in 2017.
PSO is classified as a metaheuristic because it makes few or no assumptions about the problem being optimized.
PSO can search very large spaces of candidate solutions.
PSO does not use the objective function's gradient.
PSO does not require the objective function to be differentiable.
Gradient descent requires differentiability.
Quasi-Newton methods require differentiability.
PSO does not guarantee that it will find an optimal solution.
A basic PSO run starts with a connected population of candidate solutions.
Each candidate solution in basic PSO is a numeric vector whose entries are coordinates in the search space.
A neighborhood can contain only a subset of the other particles.
The next position of a particle is determined partly at random.
A particle's personal best is updated when its new position gives a better objective value.
Repetition is expected to produce a satisfactory solution eventually, but even a satisfactory solution is not guaranteed.
The formal algorithm presented is for minimizing a cost function.
The cost function takes a vector of n real numbers as input.
The cost function returns a single real number that measures the candidate solution's objective value.
The formal setup assumes that the cost function's gradient is unknown.
A global minimizer has a cost no higher than the cost of any other point in the search space.
The notation S denotes the number of particles in the swarm.
Each particle's position is an n-dimensional real vector.
Each particle's velocity is an n-dimensional real vector.
The notation p_i denotes particle i's personal best position.
The notation g denotes the best known position in the particle's neighborhood.
The algorithm initializes each position by sampling uniformly between the lower and upper search-space bounds.
Each particle's initial position becomes its initial personal best.
During initialization, a particle's personal best replaces the swarm's recorded best if it has strictly lower cost.
Each initial velocity component is sampled uniformly from a symmetric interval whose limits are plus and minus the width of the corresponding search-space dimension.
The main loop processes every particle in each iteration.
For each dimension of each particle, the algorithm draws two random factors uniformly between zero and one.
The velocity update retains the old velocity multiplied by the inertia weight w.
The velocity update adds the displacement toward the personal best multiplied by the cognitive coefficient and one random factor.
The velocity update adds the displacement toward the neighborhood best multiplied by the social coefficient and the other random factor.
The algorithm updates a particle's position by adding its new velocity to its current position.
In the main loop, a new personal best replaces the swarm's recorded best if its cost is strictly lower.
The notation b_lo denotes the lower search-space boundary.
The notation b_up denotes the upper search-space boundary.
The parameter phi_p is commonly called the cognitive coefficient.
The parameter phi_g is commonly called the social coefficient.
A PSO run can stop after a specified number of iterations.
A PSO run can stop when it finds a solution with an adequate objective value.
In basic PSO, the practitioner selects the inertia weight and the cognitive and social coefficients.
Parameter choices can substantially affect PSO's behavior and optimization performance.
Choosing PSO parameters that perform well has been the subject of much research.
The article states that the inertia weight must be below one to prevent divergence, also called explosion.
The cognitive and social coefficients can be derived using the constriction approach.
The cognitive and social coefficients can also be chosen directly.
Convergence analyses suggest ranges that can guide the choice of the cognitive and social coefficients.
Typical values for the cognitive and social coefficients are between one and three.
Using another optimizer to tune PSO parameters is called meta-optimization.
Some PSO variants adjust parameters during a run.
Fuzzy logic is one way to adjust PSO parameters during a run.
PSO parameters have been tuned for different optimization scenarios.
Swarm topology determines which particles can exchange information with each other.
The basic algorithm uses a global communication topology, in which every particle can communicate with every other particle.
With global communication, all particles use the same best position, found by a single particle.
A global topology can cause the swarm to get stuck in a local minimum.
Alternative topologies are used to control how information flows through the swarm.
A local neighborhood can be defined geometrically, for example by taking the m closest particles.
Local neighborhoods are more often defined by social connections than by distance in the search space.
PSO with local neighborhoods is called local-best PSO, in contrast to the basic global-best PSO.
A ring is a common swarm topology.
In a ring topology, each particle has exactly two neighbors.
Ring and global topologies are not the only possible swarm topologies.
Swarm topology affects the diversity of communication among particles.
Swarm topology can change during a run.
SPSO is listed as an example of work on adaptive topologies.
APSO is listed as an example of work on adaptive topologies.
Stochastic star is listed as an example of work on adaptive topologies.
TRIBES is listed as an example of work on adaptive topologies.
Cyber Swarm is listed as an example of work on adaptive topologies.
C-PSO is listed as an example of work on adaptive topologies.
A ring topology can allow PSO to run particle updates in parallel within a generation.
Generation-level parallelism in a ring topology can substantially speed up the swarm's evolution.
Researchers have several explanations for why and how PSO works.
As particles learn from their neighbors over successive iterations, neighboring particles tend to move closer together in the search space.
As neighboring particles draw closer together, the personal-best and neighborhood-best positions tend to draw closer too.
Particles tend to take shorter steps as the swarm converges on a promising region.
Finding a new promising region late in a run can make the swarm resume exploration.
When exploration resumes after a new discovery, particles can take larger steps again.
After adapting to a discovery, particles can gradually cluster around promising regions.
The behavior of one particle is easier to understand than the behavior of the entire swarm.
According to the article, a particle on its own has no optimization ability.
One widely held view is that swarm behavior varies between exploration and exploitation.
Exploration means searching a wider region of the search space.
Exploitation means searching locally to get closer to an optimum that may only be local.
The exploration–exploitation view has been prevalent since PSO was introduced.
Under this view, the algorithm and its parameters should preserve enough exploration to avoid premature convergence on a local optimum.
Under this view, the algorithm and its parameters should also preserve enough exploitation to converge at a useful rate.
The idea of balancing exploration and exploitation inspired many PSO variants.
Another school of thought holds that the connection between swarm behavior and actual optimization performance is poorly understood.
That connection is particularly unclear in high-dimensional search spaces.
That connection is particularly unclear for discontinuous optimization problems.
That connection is particularly unclear for noisy optimization problems.
That connection is particularly unclear for problems that change over time.
The second school of thought looks for algorithms and parameters that perform well without requiring an interpretation in terms of exploration and exploitation.
Performance-focused studies have led to simplified PSO algorithms.
One meaning of convergence in PSO, studied in stability analysis, is that all particles converge to a point in the search space.
The point where all particles settle need not be an optimum.
Another meaning of convergence is that all personal bests, or alternatively the swarm's recorded best, approach a local optimum regardless of how the particles themselves behave.
Stability studies have produced guidelines for selecting parameters expected to make particles converge to a point.
The stability guidelines aim to prevent particles from moving without bound.
Pedersen criticized some PSO stability analyses for relying on overly simple assumptions.
One criticized assumption was that the swarm consisted of just one particle.
One criticized assumption was that the model used no random variables.
One criticized assumption was that the personal best stayed fixed throughout optimization.
One criticized assumption was that the swarm's best known position stayed fixed throughout optimization.
The simplifying assumptions were shown not to change the boundaries of the parameter region in which the swarm converges.
Later research has sought to weaken the assumptions required for PSO stability analysis.
The most recent generalized stability result described in the article applies to numerous PSO variants.
The most recent generalized stability result described in the article uses assumptions shown to be the minimum necessary for that result.
Analyses have proved that basic PSO must be modified to guarantee finding even a local optimum.
Assessing whether different PSO algorithms and parameter choices converge still depends on empirical results.
Orthogonal learning is one proposed strategy for improving how PSO converges.
Orthogonal learning uses information in the relationship between a particle's personal best and the swarm's best.
Orthogonal learning uses that information to construct a guiding example for convergence.
The orthogonal learning strategy is intended to work with any PSO topology.
Orthogonal learning aims to speed up global convergence.
Orthogonal learning aims to improve solution quality.
Orthogonal learning aims to improve robustness.
The orthogonal learning studies described do not theoretically establish their claimed improvements.
An adaptive mechanism is presented as a way to avoid having to set a fixed trade-off between convergent exploitation and divergent exploration.
Adaptive particle swarm optimization is reported to search more efficiently than standard PSO.
Adaptive PSO can search the entire search space globally.
Adaptive PSO can converge faster than standard PSO.
Adaptive PSO can automatically control the inertia weight while the algorithm runs.
Adaptive PSO can automatically control the acceleration coefficients while the algorithm runs.
Adaptive PSO can automatically control other algorithm settings while the algorithm runs.
Runtime parameter control in adaptive PSO is described as improving both search effectiveness and search efficiency.
Adaptive PSO can act on the globally best particle to escape a likely local optimum.
Adaptive PSO introduces additional algorithm parameters.
The article says the additional adaptive PSO parameters do not add design complexity.
The article says the additional adaptive PSO parameters do not add implementation complexity.
Scale-adaptive fitness evaluation can help PSO tackle computationally expensive optimization problems efficiently.
Many variants are possible even within the basic PSO algorithm.
PSO variants can initialize particle positions in different ways.
PSO variants can initialize velocities differently, for example by starting them at zero.
PSO variants can damp velocity in different ways.
Some variants wait until the entire swarm has been updated before updating the recorded personal and swarm bests.
Research has discussed how some of these variant choices may affect performance.
PSO researchers have created a series of standard implementations.
The standard implementations are intended to serve as baselines for testing proposed PSO improvements.
The standard implementations are intended to represent PSO to the broader optimization community.
A clearly specified standard algorithm gives researchers a common comparison point for testing new methods.
The article identifies Standard PSO 2011, or SPSO-2011, as the latest standard implementation.
Some PSO variants target large-scale global optimization problems with more than 1,000 dimensions.
Competitive swarm optimizer, or CSO, is an example of a variant for large-scale global optimization.
Level-based learning swarm optimizer, or LLSO, is an example of a variant for large-scale global optimization.
PSO has been extended to distributed optimization problems in which multiple agents must reach consensus.
MASOIE is an example of a multi-agent consensus-based PSO variant with adaptive internal and external learning.
Researchers continue to introduce more sophisticated PSO variants to try to improve optimization performance.
One research trend is to combine PSO with other optimizers to create hybrid methods.
Combining PSO with biogeography-based optimization is an example of hybridization.
Incorporating an effective learning method is another way researchers seek to improve PSO variants.
Another research trend is to prevent premature convergence, also described as optimization stagnation.
Reversing particle movement is one proposed way to reduce premature convergence.
Perturbing particle movement is another proposed way to reduce premature convergence.
Using multiple swarms is another proposed way to reduce premature convergence.
Multiple swarms can also be used for multi-objective optimization.
One school of thought favors making PSO as simple as possible without sacrificing performance, an application of Occam's razor.
Kennedy originally proposed simplifying PSO.
Further studies suggested that simplifying PSO could improve optimization performance.
Further studies suggested that simplified PSO parameters were easier to tune.
Further studies suggested that simplified PSO parameters performed more consistently across different optimization problems.
An argument for simplification is that metaheuristic effectiveness is demonstrated empirically through computational tests on a finite set of problems.
The article argues that finite empirical tests cannot prove that a metaheuristic works correctly in general.
The limits of empirical testing make errors in the description of a metaheuristic a concern.
The limits of empirical testing make errors in the implementation of a metaheuristic a concern.
A seemingly promising variant of a genetic algorithm was later found to be defective.
Genetic algorithms are another widely used type of metaheuristic.
The defective variant favored solutions with similar values across different search-space dimensions.
That bias happened to favor the optima of the benchmark problems used to test the variant.
The bias resulted from a programming error.
The programming error was later fixed.
Initializing velocities may require extra inputs.
James Kennedy proposed Bare Bones PSO in 2003.
Bare Bones PSO updates particle positions without using velocities.
Bare Bones PSO samples each new particle position from a normal distribution.
The mean in the Bare Bones PSO update is the midpoint between the particle's personal best and the global best.
The standard deviation in the Bare Bones PSO update is the norm of the difference between the personal best and the global best.
Accelerated particle swarm optimization is a simplified variant that does not use particle velocities.
Accelerated PSO also does not use each particle's personal best.
Accelerated PSO can converge more quickly in many applications.
Simple demonstration code is available for accelerated PSO.
The accelerated PSO update weights the current position by one minus beta.
The accelerated PSO update weights the global best position by beta.
The accelerated PSO update adds a uniformly distributed random vector scaled by alpha and a characteristic length of the problem.
The stated range for beta in accelerated PSO is approximately 0.1 to 0.7.
The stated range for alpha in accelerated PSO is approximately 0.1 to 0.5.
A refinement of accelerated PSO reduces alpha by multiplying its initial value by gamma raised to the iteration number.
The decay parameter gamma is strictly between zero and one.
PSO has been applied to problems with multiple objectives.
Multi-objective PSO can use Pareto dominance to compare solutions when moving particles.
Multi-objective PSO stores nondominated solutions to approximate the Pareto front.
The standard PSO movement equations operate on real numbers.
One common way to solve a discrete problem with PSO is to map the discrete search space into a continuous domain.
In this approach, standard PSO is applied in the continuous domain.
The resulting solution is mapped back to the discrete domain.
Rounding is a simple way to map continuous values back to discrete values.
Discrete PSO mappings can be more sophisticated than rounding.
Subtracting one position from another gives a displacement used in the movement equations.
The movement equations multiply a velocity by a numerical coefficient.
The movement equations add velocities together.
The movement equations apply a velocity to a position.
With real-valued vectors, the four movement operations are subtraction, scalar multiplication, vector addition, and addition of a velocity to a position.
Positions, velocities, and movement operators can be redefined to handle binary or other discrete problems.
Positions, velocities, and movement operators can also be redefined to handle combinatorial problems.
Set-based operators are one way to redefine PSO movement.

question.text: A PSO run ends with all particles settling at the same point, but a nearby point has a lower cost. What does this tell you about convergence in that run?
options: The run has reached a local optimum because all particles agree on a point.
The particle positions have converged, but that does not mean the point they settled on is a local optimum.
The particle positions cannot have converged, because convergence requires them to reach the global minimum.
The run must still be exploring, because a better point exists nearby.
